_README: Round 3 of source removal: pointers whose OBJECT is a document or a site. Rounds 1-2 used a deny-list of phrasings and were evaded by one more adjective; this rule tests the object instead - a DOCUMENT is a source, PEOPLE are not.

set.overview: Cinderella Peak (roughly 6,400-6,500 ft) is a minor summit on the south side of the Green Creek cirque in the Twin Sisters Range, immediately west of Mount Baker and within/adjacent to the Mount Baker Wilderness (Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest). The Twin Sisters massif is the largest exposed body of dunite/olivine rock in the Western Hemisphere, giving Cinderella and its neighbors (Little Sister, South Twin, Skookum, Jaws' Tooth) their signature reddish, ultra-grippy slabs. The standard route is a long approach via the Elbow Lake Trail and the unmaintained, blue-flagged Green Creek climbers' trail, gaining a saddle near Little Sister and following the connecting ridge onto Cinderella's west ridge for a final Class 3-4 scramble to the summit. Technical alternatives exist for parties wanting a real climb: a North Face route (5.2, Grade II, ~8 pitches) and an East Buttress line have both been climbed and reported. Cinderella is also a common link-up on the 'Green Creek Circuit,' which strings together South Twin, Jaws' Tooth, Skookum, Little Sister and Cinderella into a long (~11-13 mile, ~8,000 ft gain) day.

set.descent_text: This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappelling is required or typically used on the standard North Slopes route. Reverse the summit cleft and cable-protected ledge back down to the top of the Edelweiss lift station (rebuilt as a new triple chair in January 2026), taking care on the down-sloping ledge traverse (it is more exposure-sensitive descending than ascending). From there, most parties drop into Edelweiss Bowl rather than exactly retracing the International runs: descend the open bowl, cross east through Midway Saddle, and finish down Debbie's Gold ski run back to the base area, glissading or boot-skiing the snow where conditions allow — this is faster than downclimbing the steep Upper International pitch and is the descent line most parties use (roughly 1.3 hours down versus 2.5–2.7 hours up). In low-snow/summer conditions without a glissade path, simply reverse the ascent line of least resistance back through the ski-slope brush and scree to the base lodge, watching for loose rock and the same route-finding ambiguity encountered on the way up. Hazards on descent are exposure on the cable ledge, potential glissade-path hazards (rocks, run-out onto talus) in Edelweiss Bowl, and loose/scree footing lower down; no technical rope work is needed on this route.

set.approach: From the Phelps Creek Trailhead (elev. ~3,500 ft, at the end of Phelps Creek Road/FR-6211), follow the Phelps Creek Trail (FST 1511) north up the east side of Phelps Creek through old-growth and second-growth forest. The trail crosses several small side streams (reliable water the whole way) and, in years with heavy winter avalanche activity, threads through 'graveyards' of downed timber deposited across the tread by slide paths off the Ten Peak/Chipmunk Creek slopes to the west — expect some minor scrambling over debris and a couple of ankle-to-shin stream fords early season. The trail climbs gently, gaining roughly 1,900 ft over about 6-7 miles to reach Spider Meadow (~5,400 ft), a broad subalpine meadow with good campsites and the last easy, reliable water before the basin. At the head of the meadow the trail forks: the left branch continues toward Spider Gap/Larch Knob, while climbers bound for Dumbell should watch for the unsigned climbers' path (old FST 1511A) that splits right (east) about 0.3 mile into lower Phelps Basin. Most parties camp in upper Phelps Basin (~6,000 ft), 8-9 miles and roughly 2,500 ft above the trailhead. From camp, leave the last of the boot path and head east/northeast up along a tumbling side creek that cuts through an otherwise cliffy face, following a broad talus-and-scree gully on the south side of Dumbell. Grass and heather give way to talus and (through roughly mid-August) moderate snow as you climb into the basin directly south of the summit. Gain the southeast ridge/shoulder at a distinct notch, then work up steep snow or a loose scree-and-talus gully 100-200 yards left (west) of the notch to reach a system of ledges; these ledges zig-zag up onto the west ridge, which is then followed a few hundred feet of easy but moderately exposed Class 3 scrambling to the 8,421-ft summit. Route-finding is the main crux — several parallel gullies and ledge systems exist and it's easy to get cliffed out on the wrong one — and loose rock, lingering steep snow (an ice axe and sometimes crampons are worth carrying into July), and a reported unstable, truck-sized snow block perched on a slab near 8,000 ft in the direct south-face gully are all real hazards on this line. A longer alternate approach reaches the same basin from the east via Railroad Creek/Lyman Lake and Spider Gap out of Holden Village on Lake Chelan — considerably longer, typically used by parties already doing the Lyman Lake/Spider Gap loop.

set.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line — this is a walk-off/downclimb, not a rappel route. From the summit, downclimb the same Class 2 (right side) or Class 2/3 (center) slope back down about 600 vertical feet to the ~5,000 ft bench, then reverse the counterclockwise talus traverse below the cliff bands back to treeline, and continue down through open forest and brush to the FR-6517 parking area. No technical anchors or rappels are needed on the standard line. The main descent hazards are loose talus/scree (easy to kick rocks onto anyone below) and route-finding — in poor visibility it's easy to drift toward the cliff bands instead of holding the correct counterclockwise line, so retrace your ascent traverse carefully. Parties who climbed the more exposed far-left finish (about 50 ft of slightly exposed Class 3) sometimes downclimb that section more cautiously or carry ~50 ft of rope to rig an optional handline for extra security, but this is a personal-comfort choice on a minor variation, not a fixed rappel station, and the standard Class 2/3 line requires no rope at all.

set.beta: Widely described as 'nothing more than a walk' once the Lucky Pass col is reached — the difficulty of this route lies almost entirely in the approach (creek crossing, steep brushy ridge gain, and a glacier traverse), not the summit scramble itself. Most parties treat it as a 2-3 day backcountry trip out of Colonial Creek Campground.

set.descent_text: Descend by reversing the southeast ridge/gully line used on ascent: downclimb class 2–3 terrain from the summit block back to the notch in the upper basin between Saska and Emerald, then follow the gully back down to the 6,900 ft basin and re-cross the shoulder to the camp flat near 7,000–7,100 ft. This is a walk-off/downclimb — no fixed anchors or rappel stations are reported on this route, and parties climbing the Saska–Emerald–Cardinal group describe simul-downclimbing or careful scrambling rather than rappelling, since the class 2-3 terrain generally isn't steep or exposed enough to require rope work. The main descent hazards are loose, blocky rock in the gully (rockfall risk onto parties below, and ankle-turning talus/scree lower down) and, in early season, moderate snow in the gully requiring an ice axe and possibly crampons — parties have noted lingering snow patches into summer. From the basin, retrace the cross-country line back to the Pyramid Mountain Trail junction and descend the North Fork Entiat River Trail #1437 the full ~9 miles back to the trailhead, watching footing on the same deadfall and creek crossings encountered on the way in (a crampon-related slip near the final miles has been reported, so stay attentive even on the "easy" trail portion when fatigued). If any party member is uncomfortable with the exposure in the gully/notch section, a short hand-line or single rappel off natural gear (block/horn) could reasonably be rigged, but this is not standard practice for the route.

This is a walk-off/glacier descent with no rappelling — reverse the ascent line. From the summit, descend the pumice Sitkum ridge back to the ~9,500 ft saddle east of Sitkum Spire, then descend the Sitkum Glacier's upper section, staying in the corridor left of the icefall/rock rib that splits the glacier's lower half, back down to Boulder Basin. Crevasses exist on the Sitkum but are sparse and generally avoidable with standard route-finding; a rope, harness, and a few pickets are still standard kit. From Boulder Basin, follow the steep climbers' path back down to the PCT/White Chuck Trail junction and retrace the White Chuck River Trail to the trailhead. Set rappels to 0.

North Rib tops out on the same summit ridge system as Guye's other routes, so the descent is the standard south-to-north traverse/rappel sequence rather than a reversal of the climbing line. From the summit reached, scramble/downclimb toward the notch between the middle and north summits, where fixed rappel rings are already slung/bolted into the rock — enough parties found the step steep enough to rig it permanently that a rope-assisted descent (roughly 30-40 ft, single strand or doubled off a shorter rope) is the norm rather than the exception. If your line tops out further south, you'll first need to negotiate the notch between the south and middle summits, which is loose mossy class 3/4 slab commonly rappelled off tree-sling anchors (30-60 ft). A related variation sometimes climbed on this side of the peak, the 'Hidden Ridge' line, itself uses a short 30-40 ft rappel mid-route (leaving the rope in place and top-roping back up), which can add confusion about anchor locations if you're relying on other parties' beta — the rap rings at the middle/north notch are the ones relevant to a normal summit-to-car descent. From the north summit, follow the well-defined scrambler's trail down past a small pond, then swing west back to the Alpental lot. Carry a single 30m+ rope, rap device, and a prussik/cordelette to back up any weathered slings; expect climber-triggered rockfall risk in the gullies, worse when snow patches remain into early summer (the steep gullies here can hold snow into a normal season and feel considerably more serious with snow in them than the bare-rock class 3 of summer conditions).

set.beta: Sometimes given simply as 'North Route, class 3-4', this line is also known as North Ridge - North Cirque - Northeast Ridge, and it is the way to do the North Peak as a day climb from the US side. From the Hozomeen ranger station at about 1,600 ft, take the short Trail of the Obelisk loop, then break off cross-country to the east, cross Howlett Creek and grind up through moderately open forest on the mountain's western flank. Gain the north ridge at a heathery knoll around 5,900 ft, then follow the ridge south over several bumps - the left side of the crest is a fun Class 2-3 scramble on comparatively good rock. Near 6,800 ft the ridge intersects the upper mountain; drop about 250 ft into the lower snowfields of the north cirque, climb them, and finish on the northeast ridge exactly as the Northeast Buttress route does, including the eroded, very exposed Class 4 segment near 7,600 ft. Above that the crest is Class 2-3 to the summit.

set.descent_text: Descent reverses the ascent line: downclimb the loose red-tinged rock, dirt, and scree of the south face/summit tower back to the talus benches above Iron Cap Lake basin, then drop back down to Dutch Miller Gap and rejoin the maintained Dutch Miller Gap/Middle Fork Trail (#1030/#1003) for the long walk out to the Dingford Creek Trailhead. This is a class 2–3 scramble route with no fixed anchors or rappel stations — it is a walk-off/downclimb, not a rappel descent. The main hazards on the way down are the same loose, dirt-over-rock terrain that makes the ascent's crux (test holds carefully, especially when wet or in the early season with residual snow patches), plus the route-finding challenge of picking the correct gully/ledge system back down to the basin rather than getting cliffed out on the steeper east-side rock bands — parties in this area have reported wandering into steep 'veggie' terrain when they lost the correct line, so retracing your ascent track (or using a GPS track) is the most reliable way down. Once back at Dutch Miller Gap, it's a straightforward, well-graded trail walk of roughly 15 miles back to the trailhead with the elevation loss front-loaded near the gap and gentler grades through the lower valley.

set.beta: An enjoyable alpine route, and the most direct of the three approaches to Kyes. From the northeast base of the peak (~6,000 ft), Class 3 rock along the climber's-left edge of the Pride Glacier leads to the summit via its southeast corner. Glacier travel (crevasses reported) and route-finding through Quartz Basin's cliff bands on the approach add seriousness beyond the rock grade alone.

set.descent_text: No descent is described anywhere for this route, which is the single biggest gap in what is known about it. What is known about the mountain's geography suggests the options: from the top of the west face, the southwest slopes lead back down to the outflow of Lake Valhalla at class 2, and the northeast side drops toward Lichtenwasser Lake at 4,708 ft on similarly easy ground — both of these are established walking descents used by the peak's scramble routes. There are no fixed anchors, bolts or rappel stations recorded anywhere on Lichtenberg Mountain, so a party planning to rappel the line should expect to build and leave their own gear. Confirm your descent plan by eye from the lake before you commit to the wall.

set.beta: This is a remoteness-and-navigation objective more than a technical one — the documented 'easiest route' is class 3 (YDS) scrambling with no reported roped climbing, but it sits far off any maintained trail. No other named technical route (rock face, ridge, or couloir line) is documented on this peak; the subsidiary East Peak (8,160+ ft) was reached separately in 1940 by Fred Beckey's party, likely by a similar approach but not confirmed as the same exact line.

There is no maintained trail on Mount Barnes itself. Parties approach via the long Elwha River Trail to a camp in or near Elwha Basin, then leave the trail entirely and travel cross-country up open slopes/heather benches toward the summit ridge, following the class 2 line. No rope or rack is used on the standard line; the challenge is routefinding and the length/remoteness of the approach, not technical difficulty.

set.overview: A striking, roughly 2,000 ft alpine granite ridge climb up Berge's east side - sustained low-to-mid 5th class rock broken by one 5.8 chimney crux - comparable in quality and length to the Complete North Ridge of Mount Stuart.

set.beta: Recorded by its first-ascent party only as a new, relatively short route on the East Face of Mt Bigelow, climbed at 5.10c on August 23, 2011. No pitch count, protection details, or topo are available.

set.approach: From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead (2,500 ft, end of FR 2870; USFS day-use fee/permit required), start on the Upper Dungeness Trail (FST 833). The trail climbs gently through old-growth forest along the Dungeness River; at about 1 mile it reaches Royal Creek and the junction with the Royal Basin Trail (FST 832) — bear right/south onto FST 832 and follow Royal Creek upstream. The trail climbs gradually through forest, transitioning to open rocky, brushy terrain above roughly 4,000 ft, then reaches Royal Lake (5,100 ft) at about 6-7 miles from the trailhead (~2,500-2,600 ft gain to this point) — the last reliable, easy water and a common overnight camp for a 2-3 day itinerary. From the lake, circle to its far end and continue past Shelter Rock, a large pillow-lava overhang used as a rough bivy shelter, then through a meadow with a waterfall and along the outlet stream into Upper Royal Basin (~5,600-5,700 ft), roughly 1 more mile and 500 ft of gain — another good camp and water source (snowmelt tarns/stream, treat before drinking). From the upper basin tarn, leave the trail and climb southwest across a glacial moraine (~1 mile) to the base of a large snow (or, late-season, mud/scree) slope on the west edge of Deception's northeast face; this slope leads up toward the Deception-Martin saddle and the remnant Deception Glacier. Route-finding on the moraine and lower slope is straightforward but the rock throughout the upper mountain is loose, rotten pillow lava — helmet mandatory from here up, and watch for rockfall triggered by parties above. Above the saddle, descend/traverse about 100 ft onto the glacier remnant and work westward around Gilhooley Tower and adjoining crags (go around to the west — do not try to climb over) to reach class 2 slopes leading to the summit; the alternate line through Surprise Basin avoids the steepest ground but is long, arduous, and not recommended.
set.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line: from the summit, walk the class 2 slopes back around the west side of Gilhooley Tower and the adjoining crags, regain the Deception-Martin saddle area, and descend the same snow/mud/scree slope back onto the upper moraine and into Upper Royal Basin. This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble descent with no rappelling required anywhere on the standard route — no fixed anchors, bolts, or rap stations are reported on this line. The steep upper slope is the crux of the descent: several parties describe it as loose rock, hard mud, and rotten scree in late-season/low-snow conditions (not a place to slip — a fall could be hard to arrest given the loose surface), while a lingering snowfield/snow-finger makes for a faster, more secure glissade-and-plunge-step descent earlier in the season. Stay well clear of Gilhooley Tower's east/direct side on the way down, as steep ground there has been the site of serious injuries; the safe line goes around to the west as on the ascent. From Upper Royal Basin, retrace the approach: back down past Shelter Rock to Royal Lake, then out FST 832/FST 833 to the Upper Dungeness Trailhead.

This is a walk-off/glacier-descent route with no rappelling on file — set rappels to 0. Descend by reversing the ascent line: from the summit, recross the Fairchild Glacier roped up with crampons, following the same wind-formed snow ridge back down to the ~6,700 ft access point, then regain Mount Carrie's north-side ridge. Sidehill/traverse back across the Catwalk (or the north-side alternative) to Cat Basin, drop to rejoin the maintained High Divide Trail at the Cat Basin junction (~10.2 mi mark), and retrace the trail past the Seven Lakes Basin junction, Bogachiel Peak, Potholes Meadows, Deer Lake, and Lovers Lane back down to Sol Duc Falls and the Sol Duc River Trailhead. Some parties instead continue the descent onward as part of the broader Bailey Range Traverse — dropping south past Ruth Peak toward Stephen Lake/Queets Basin and exiting via the Elwha (Whiskey Bend) or Hoh River trailheads — but that is a different, longer one-way multi-day itinerary rather than the out-and-back standard route matching this route's on-file distance and gain. Descent hazards mirror the approach: crevasse fall potential on the glacier (softening snow in the afternoon raises post-holing/slot risk, so an early turnaround is wise), loose talus on the Carrie sidehill, fatigue-driven route-finding errors in the featureless heather and scree of Cat Basin, and long, tired-legs reversal of the steep Deer Lake Trail switchbacks.

set.approach: From the Cascade Pass Trailhead (3,600 ft) at the end of Cascade River Road, follow the maintained Cascade Pass Trail 3.7 miles and about 1,800 ft of gain to Cascade Pass (5,392 ft) — a well-graded trail, roughly 1.5-2 hours at a steady pace. This is the last maintained tread; everything beyond is boot-path/climbers'-trail, the start of the Ptarmigan Traverse. From the pass, leave the trail and climb/contour east and north below Cache Ridge toward Cache Col (~6,903 ft), crossing the toe of the Cache Glacier — generally a mellow, low-crevasse-hazard crossing in early/mid season but rope up if it's opened out or snow-covered, since crevasse hazard has caught parties off guard here in low-snow years. From Cache Col, descend a talus traverse on a good climbers' trail down to Kool-Aid Lake (6,100 ft), a small meltwater tarn that is the standard base camp for the route (no permit required, no fires) — roughly 3 hours and 5-6 miles from Cascade Pass, so plan on 5-7 hours trailhead-to-camp overall. From Kool-Aid Lake continue south past Art's Knoll to the broad, well-known 'Red Ledge' — an exposed traverse over loose rock and (often) lingering snow patches that many parties choose to rope for; it is the most consistently reported crux of the approach and is noticeably worse when snow-covered. Beyond Red Ledge, follow a rough climbers' path roughly a mile over meadows, snow, talus, and small rock ribs toward the Middle Cascade Glacier icefall (~6,500 ft), then rope up and ascend the glacier's left/SSE side, weaving through crevasses, to the Spider-Formidable col (7,320 ft). From the col, descend/traverse (plunge-stepping snow, crampons for icy sections) to a flat camp/staging area below the south face snow slope near a notch around 7,050 ft — this is the jump-off point for the climb proper. From there the final approach to the route gains the south-face snowfield alcove via one of two options: a hidden gully on the left (reportedly with 5th-class moves) or, more commonly, a winding ledge on the right rated 3rd class with one 3rd-class-plus section. Water is available at Kool-Aid Lake and from glacier meltwater streams along the Middle Cascade Glacier margins; carry enough for the long, exposed traverse sections beyond. Overall this is a long, remote glacier-and-ledge approach with real route-finding demands — most parties treat it as a 2-3 day trip with camp at Kool-Aid Lake or the south-face notch rather than a single push.

set.descent_text: The North Face is not descended — after topping out on the summit ridge (9,082 ft), descend via the standard South Slopes / south ridge walk-off: down the south ridge and upper talus to about 7,700 ft, then southwest down broad open slopes to the 6,840 ft saddle. From there most parties drop back into Leroy Creek Basin to retrieve camp and reverse the Leroy Creek climber's path and Phelps Creek Trail to the trailhead; some parties instead exit via the Ice Lakes basin and the Carne Mountain High Route depending on snow conditions and where camp/vehicles are staged, which several parties describe as an efficient alternative when the Maude/Seven Fingered Jack col has gone soft and mushy in the afternoon. This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappelling is required or commonly reported on the standard descent line, so rappels is set to 0 for the route's descent proper (the single technical rappel reported is on the approach traverse under the face, not the summit descent, and is conditions-dependent rather than a fixed feature of the route). Descent-specific hazards: loose 3rd-class rock and scree on the south ridge/upper slopes, a large cornice that forms on the summit ridge above the North Face's climber's-right side (stay well back from the edge near the top), lingering steep snow and possible rockfall in the col/gully area, and — if exiting toward Ice Lakes — extra route-finding and a longer, more remote tail to the car. Parties should budget real time for this descent; one party logged roughly 13 hours car-to-car including the North Face climb and this walk-off.

Descend by reversing the ascent line rather than a separate walk-off. From the true summit, downclimb the short exposed crest/corkscrew section back to the top of the summit block's crux pitch. Two independent parties describe needing two rappels here to get down the steep upper step of the southeast ridge/northeast face terrain (the same short low-5th-class face and exposed crest climbed on the way up) before a final downclimb/traverse regains the sloping ledge and the Meany-Noyes col. Anchors reported here are natural/improvised - slung horns, blocks, or a hand-placed piton in a crack - not bolted or fixed hardware, so carry a small rack (stoppers, a few pitons or a hammer if you want backup, and slings) for building gauge anchors; do not expect anything pre-equipped. Given the short pitch heights described (a roughly 25-foot crux face and a similarly short second step), a single 30-40m rope rappelled should cover each stretch, though most parties simply carry their climbing rope (commonly a 30-60m single) and rappel it as a single strand or doubled depending on length and anchor position - exact rope length isn't specified, so size it to your rack and be ready to build an intermediate anchor if a single rappel doesn't reach. Below the rappels, reverse the loose rock couloir and the scree/dirt sidehill beneath Mt. Noyes back to the Noyes-Meany saddle, then cross-country back down to Seattle Basin camp. From there, reverse the full approach: Skyline route down to Low Divide, the North Fork Quinault ford, and the North Fork Quinault River Trail back to the trailhead. Loose rock on the couloir and sidehill, and the exposed, unprotected downclimbing between the rappels, are the primary descent hazards - this is not a beginner scramble descent despite the 'scrambling' classification.

set.beta: From the Dingford Creek Trailhead, follow the Dingford Creek Trail (multiple creek crossings) toward Hester Lake and Little Hester Lake — roughly the first 5-6 miles. Leave the trail and make an ascending traverse below cliff bands, climbing a short, steep gully along Price Creek between about 3,200 and 3,800 ft — reported by multiple parties as the most technical part of the scramble. From the lakes basin, ascend the boulder field south of Little Hester Lake to gain Price's east ridge near Point 5,480'/5,440', traverse the steep north side of the ridge to a col around 5,400 ft just east of the true summit, and finish with a short ridge scramble to the 5,587 ft summit. Expect Class 3 scrambling with occasional steep snow or rock gullies on the ridge, and real routefinding difficulty — at least one party's own GPS track diverged noticeably between ascent and descent.
Grade I, Class 3 via Noyes Basin — an off-trail scramble approach with no glacier travel, distinct from the Low Divide and Seattle Creek Basin lines on the same peak.
Grade I, Class 3 via Seattle Creek Basin — an off-trail scramble approach with no glacier travel, distinct from the Low Divide and Noyes Basin lines on the same peak.

Moderate rock climbing between 4th class and 5.7 gains the exposed summit block; it requires additional ice climbing lower down to reach the base of the ridge and complex alpine rock-finding higher up. It is generally regarded as an alternate finish rather than a fully independent line from base to summit.

set.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line: down the summit scree/rock to the saddle, then back along the boot path traverse across scree/grass/rock benches around the south and east flanks to the 5,800-ft saddle above Lake of the Angels, down to the lake, and out the Putvin Trail to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb - there is no rappelling on the standard scramble route, so rappels = 0. The main descent hazard is the same rotten rock and loose scree that makes the ascent tricky: downclimbing the exposed class 3 sections near the summit ridge crest is generally regarded as harder and more hazard-prone than climbing them, and parties should stay well left/south of the steeper cliffy drop-off noted on the north side of the upper mountain (parties specifically warn that contouring too far right/north near the ridge crest 'gets sketchy, exposed, and dangerous' and to cut west over the ridge instead). Watch for rockfall onto climbers below on the scree/talus sections, expect residual snow in the gullies and on the traverse into early summer (ice axe/crampons may be warranted), and budget real time for careful downclimbing rather than assuming a fast glissade-style descent - one party logged about 2.5 hours from summit back to the trailhead, but that was in good, snow-free conditions.

set.beta: From Crescent Creek Basin, ascend broad granite slabs up toward the saddle between Mount Terror and Mount Degenhardt, then follow the short, steep summit ridge directly to the top — described as offering 'challenges beyond that of a normal alpine rock climb' despite its modest 5.6 rating, due to looseness and exposure on the upper ridge.

set.approach: From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead (~2,960 ft, end of FR 2870), start on the Upper Dungeness Trail #833.2, which runs a gentle, mostly level mile through old-growth forest along the Dungeness River to a well-signed junction. Bear right (east, then south) onto the Royal Basin Trail #840 and settle into a steady, moderate climb up the Royal Creek valley for about 5 miles, crossing several tributary creeks — the last reliable water before the high basin — through forest that opens into wildflower meadows around the 6-mile mark, with Mount Clark and Mount Walkinshaw's 7,000-ft summits visible ahead. The trail steepens for the final push through switchbacks into Royal Basin, reaching Royal Lake (5,100 ft, ~7.2 mi, ~2,500 ft gain) — the established backcountry camp area (bear canisters required, no fires, permits needed May-Sept). From the lake, a climbers' path continues roughly another 0.8-1 mile and 500 ft of gain across willow flats and boulder benches to Upper Royal Basin (~5,600 ft, ~8 mi from the trailhead), the base camp used for all Needles-area objectives. Beyond Upper Royal Basin there is no maintained tread: traverse cross-country north, contouring below Mount Clark's east flank on talus and boulder benches toward Mount Walkinshaw, the northernmost peak in the Needles chain — this stretch is rough, adds roughly 1.5 miles and several hundred feet of ascending/descending sidehill travel, and involves genuine route-finding (krummholz and short cliff bands can obscure the best line, as noted by parties working this same traverse from the Gray Wolf Ridge side). Aim for the prominent talus tongue and gully system on Walkinshaw's east/southeast side — this is the 'West Side' class-3 scramble route. Ascend the loose, blocky gully (described firsthand as 'rotten Olympic shale' — notably looser than typical Cascades granite) with care, then follow class 2-3 terrain along the upper ridge, including a few short class-3 moves past steepened pinnacles, to the small (~10-ft-diameter) rocky summit at 7,378 ft. Keep parties tight and helmets on through the entire gully/ridge section — loose rock and rockfall onto climbers below are the defining hazard of this route. Total round-trip distance from the trailhead is on the order of 19 miles (matching the route's on-file 30.58 km), reflecting the extra cross-country mileage beyond Upper Royal Basin that standard figures for the closer Royal Basin peaks (Deception/Mystery, ~14 mi RT) don't include.

The drive itself is easy — paved the whole way from Winthrop up the Chewuch River valley to the Andrews Creek Trailhead, about 28 miles total — but the climb to Cathedral Peak is one of the longest wilderness approaches in the state. From the trailhead, the Andrews Creek Trail (#504) climbs roughly 12 miles to 6,680+ ft Andrews Pass, then descends into the Spanish Creek drainage before a side trail climbs to Upper Cathedral Lakes below the peak's southwest side, putting the one-way approach at around 18 miles with significant elevation gain and loss along the way. Most parties treat this as a 2-4 day backpack (roughly 40+ miles round trip), camping at or near Cathedral Lakes before making a summit push. A free self-issue wilderness permit is required at the trailhead, along with a trailhead parking pass; the first many miles are a hot, rocky, buggy uphill slog with little shade, so this is genuinely a remote, multi-day alpine objective rather than a day-approach crag. For this specific route: from Cathedral Lakes camp, follow the trail toward Cathedral Pass and climb scree/talus to the base of the peak's main South Face; SE Buttress starts on the left wall just after entering the deep gully that separates Cathedral Peak from The Monk, while NE Ridge is gained by continuing up and around toward the ridgeline running north.

The drive itself is easy — paved the whole way from Winthrop up the Chewuch River valley to the Andrews Creek Trailhead, about 28 miles total — but the climb to Cathedral Peak is one of the longest wilderness approaches in the state. From the trailhead, the Andrews Creek Trail (#504) climbs roughly 12 miles to 6,680+ ft Andrews Pass, then descends into the Spanish Creek drainage before a side trail climbs to Upper Cathedral Lakes below the peak's southwest side, putting the one-way approach at around 18 miles with significant elevation gain and loss along the way. Most parties treat this as a 2-4 day backpack (roughly 40+ miles round trip), camping at or near Cathedral Lakes before making a summit push. A free self-issue wilderness permit is required at the trailhead, along with a trailhead parking pass; the first many miles are a hot, rocky, buggy uphill slog with little shade, so this is genuinely a remote, multi-day alpine objective rather than a day-approach crag. For this specific route: from Cathedral Lakes camp, follow the trail toward Cathedral Pass and climb scree/talus to the base of the peak's main South Face; SE Buttress starts on the left wall just after entering the deep gully that separates Cathedral Peak from The Monk, while NE Ridge is gained by continuing up and around toward the ridgeline running north.

set.beta: From the col between Vesper and Sperry Peaks, an obvious ledge system cuts across the north face at roughly 5,800 ft, starting at a small notch overlooking the Vesper Glacier. The climbing is sustained low-5th-class rock with the crux exposed traverse pitch reported on pitch 5 (some parties also flag a 5.7 slab on pitch 2); belays are a mix of fixed (bolted/pin) anchors and gear anchors atop pitches 1 and 3. No rappels are needed — parties walk off. Popular enough that other Vesper lines (e.g. True Grit) are sometimes used as a less-crowded backup.

set.overview: A winter/spring line up Ruby's north side following the Happy Creek drainage — the least demanding way up the mountain in the right snow conditions.

A pair of pyramidal twin summits in the Entiat Mountains subrange of the North Cascades, within the Glacier Peak Wilderness on Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Wenatchee River Ranger District) land in Chelan County. The sharper south summit (8,392 ft) is the true high point; the north butte (8,080 ft) sits about a half-mile away across a connecting basin. The name comes from their twin-lensed profile as seen from the Entiat River valley. First ascent of the south peak was made August 20, 1953 by Rowland Tabor and Dwight Crowder. This route follows the southwest ridge/west-facing slopes — the standard line on South Spectacle Butte — reached via a long, mostly cross-country approach through Leroy Basin and the Ice Lakes basin. Traffic is light; most parties combine it with Ice Lakes camping or a Leroy-Carne loop.

set.beta: After camping at Spectacle Point (5,800 ft), the route climbs the West Ridge and West Face of West Peak to the summit — described simply as 'rock scramble and rock climb,' i.e. class 3-4 terrain without a documented technical crux comparable to the Middle Peak chimney.

set.overview: A 5.8 trad rock line developed by Darin Berdinka on Vesper Peak's north face in 2015, reached via the same ledge-system access as Ragged Edge; a quieter alternative when Ragged Edge is crowded.
